name: Narragansett Bay and Block Island
blurb: Eelgrass, menhaden and shellfish feeding bass, ospreys and whales.

tip.title: Add more nitrogen
tip.text: Nitrogen feeds the bay's algae. Raise Nitrogen from land and sewage by 100% and follow the change through phytoplankton, menhaden and the predators that eat them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching shallow water and marsh drives growth of algae, eelgrass and marsh plants.

nodes.name: Nitrogen from land and sewage
nodes.desc: Nitrogen is a key nutrient for the bay's algae. Cuts in wastewater nitrogen since 2006 have been followed by smaller annual phytoplankton blooms.

nodes.name: Tides and cool ocean water
nodes.desc: Tides and ocean exchange flush the bay, bringing cooler, saltier water in from Rhode Island Sound.

nodes.name: Bacteria and detritus feeders
nodes.desc: Break down dead marsh grass, eelgrass and algae, and release nutrients back into the water.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae that form the base of the food chain for many of the bay's marine animals.

nodes.name: Eelgrass
nodes.desc: Underwater meadows that shelter young fish, give mussels a place to attach and feed geese and brant.

nodes.name: Smooth cordgrass
nodes.desc: Salt-marsh grass of the tidal edge. Its dead stems feed the detritus-based part of the marsh food web.

nodes.name: Seaside goldenrod
nodes.desc: A coastal wildflower of dunes and marsh edges, common on Block Island and the Rhode Island shore.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Tiny drifting crustaceans that graze phytoplankton and are eaten by young menhaden and other small fish.

nodes.name: Atlantic menhaden
nodes.desc: A schooling filter-feeding fish. Many predators, including striped bass, bluefish, osprey and dolphins, eat it.

nodes.name: Blue mussel
nodes.desc: Filter-feeding mollusc that clings to rocks, piers and eelgrass, eating plankton.

nodes.name: Northern quahog
nodes.desc: A hard clam buried in bay sediments that filters plankton from the water. Long harvested in Rhode Island.

nodes.name: Canada goose
nodes.desc: Grazes on grasses and, as shown in other bays, on eelgrass rhizomes.

nodes.name: Meadow vole
nodes.desc: Small grass-eating rodent of fields and dunes. GloBI records link it to seaside goldenrod.

nodes.name: Striped bass
nodes.desc: An opportunistic predatory fish of the bay. Menhaden are a notable part of its diet.

nodes.name: Bluefish
nodes.desc: A fast schooling predator that hunts menhaden and other forage fish along the coast.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: A fish-eating raptor that nests around the bay; menhaden are among its prey.

nodes.name: Common eider
nodes.desc: A sea duck that winters on the coast and dives for mussels and other shellfish.

nodes.name: American herring gull
nodes.desc: Abundant coastal gull that eats shellfish, fish and scavenged carrion.

nodes.name: Common bottlenose dolphin
nodes.desc: A toothed whale that eats schooling fish such as menhaden; recorded in waters off the bay.

nodes.name: Humpback whale
nodes.desc: A baleen whale that gulps schools of small fish; it is the most recorded mammal around the bay mouth in GBIF.
